Or more precisely, *some* were and some weren't, and there was zero indication of which was which until I tapped into a page and got the spinning loader going nowhere.

The pages that did load were read-only anyway — I couldn't update statuses, couldn't check off prep tasks, couldn't add a single note. Honestly, less critical than it could be because I've *adapted around it*, which is itself a red flag. I've trained myself to pre-load pages before travel. The most painful example was trying to build a sprint review workflow that pulled GitHub PR data into our project tracker. The ask was simple: when a PR merges, update the linked task in Notion, log the deployment date, and move the status to "Shipped." In theory, Zapier should handle this. In practice, it was a nightmare. Zapier's Notion integration couldn't reliably write to relation properties — it would silently fail or create duplicate entries. - **Slack → Notion** via Zapier for capturing action items from standups. Works okay for simple text, breaks completely the moment you try to write to a select or multi-select field with any consistency

**Q1: How do you currently use Notion AI, and where does it disappoint you?**

I use Notion AI pretty regularly for a few specific things: drafting first-pass content for our internal wikis, summarizing long meeting notes, and occasionally generating action items from a wall of text. The summarization on a single page is genuinely useful — I'll drop in a 2,000-word product spec and get a clean TL;DR that I can paste into Slack. That part works.

Where it falls apart is anything requiring *context*. I'll ask it to "write a project brief" and it produces this embarrassingly generic output because it has no idea who our customers are, what our product does, or what our team's voice sounds like. I've tried feeding it context manually every single time, which completely defeats the purpose. It's like hiring a contractor who forgets everything between visits. I've also tried using it on database entries — asking it to auto-fill a "summary" property across our sprint tasks — and the quality is wildly inconsistent. Some entries are great, some are hallucinated garbage. I can't trust it enough to automate it without a review layer, which again kills the efficiency argument.

The other thing that genuinely annoys me: it can't read across linked databases. I have a project database that relations into a client database and a team capacity database. Notion AI is blind to all of that relational context when you're on any given page. It only sees what's directly in front of it.

---

**Q2: Describe a scenario where you wished Notion could reason across your entire workspace, not just one page.**

This happens to me constantly during quarterly planning. Here's the specific scenario:

I have four databases — Projects, Team Members, Clients, and Sprints. They're all relational. I'm trying to answer a seemingly simple question: *"Which team members are over-allocated next quarter based on current project assignments, and which clients will be impacted?"*

Right now I have to manually cross-reference three filtered database views, open individual team member pages, check their rollup fields, then go back to the client database and trace it forward. It takes me 45 minutes of tab-switching and mental load to produce something I could explain to you in one sentence.

If Notion AI could actually traverse those relations — understand that Jordan is linked to four active projects, that two of those projects have Q3 deadlines overlapping, that Jordan's capacity rollup shows 110% — and then surface "hey, Client X and Client Y are at risk" — that would be transformative. Instead I export everything to a spreadsheet and do it there, which is embarrassing given how much time I've invested in building this Notion infrastructure.

Linear does something closer to this with its dependency and cycle reasoning, even without AI. The fact that a purpose-built project tool reasons about connected data better than Notion's AI does frustrates me more than I can articulate politely.

---

**Q3: How does Notion AI compare to other AI tools you use in your workflow?**

Honestly, it's not the worst but it's probably the most *disappointing* relative to expectations — because Notion has all the structured data and I assumed the AI would actually use it.

I use Claude pretty heavily for anything requiring actual reasoning or drafting that needs nuance. The difference is stark. Claude doesn't have access to my workspace, but when I paste in context, it *uses* that context intelligently, makes inferences, asks clarifying questions. Notion AI feels like autocomplete with a thesaurus.

I also use Linear's built-in AI features for engineering-adjacent work, and what Linear does well is that its AI suggestions are *scoped appropriately* — it knows it's operating in a project management context and doesn't try to be everything. Notion AI seems to want to be a generalist writing assistant living inside a structured database tool, and it's not quite good enough at either job to win on either front.

The place Notion AI beats everything else is sheer *convenience* — it's right there in the doc, zero context switching for simple tasks. If I'm cleaning up a messy meeting note or reformatting a page, I'll use it because it's fast. But for anything that actually requires understanding my business or reasoning across information? I'm going somewhere else.

---

SEVERITY: 7/10
FREQUENCY: 8/10
SWITCH_LIKELIHOOD: 5/10

# My Honest Take on Notion's External Connectivity

---

## Q1: A Workflow That Should Have Been Simple

I tried to set up a basic client intake flow last year. The idea was: a potential client fills out a Typeform, and that data automatically populates a new entry in my Notion CRM — name, project type, budget range, timeline. Seemed straightforward.

I ended up spending an entire afternoon in Zapier trying to map fields, and half of them just... didn't land correctly. The budget field kept coming in as plain text instead of a number, which broke my filters. And because I was at a coffee shop with spotty wifi, I couldn't tell if the zap was failing or if Notion's API was just being slow. I ran the same test three times and got duplicate entries twice.

The thing that really frustrated me is that I'm not trying to do anything exotic. Client name goes in a field. That's it. But the path to get there — Typeform → Zapier → Notion API → correct property type — has so many places to silently fail, and Notion gives you almost no feedback when something goes wrong on its end.

I eventually got it working, but I don't fully trust it. I still manually check my CRM after every new inquiry.

---

## Q2: "Team" Is Generous, But Here's My Reality

I work solo, but I collaborate with a small rotating cast — a copywriter, a developer I refer work to, and occasionally a brand strategist. So my "integrations" are pretty personal-stack focused.

**What I rely on:**
- **Google Calendar** — Notion's calendar integration feels bolted on. I can *see* a calendar view inside Notion, but it doesn't sync bidirectionally with Google Calendar in any reliable way. I've missed meetings because I added something in Notion assuming it would show up in my phone calendar. It didn't.
- **Email** — This is the big one. I want to log client emails directly to their CRM card. There's no native way to do this. I've tried workarounds with Zapier and even briefly tried a Make.com flow, but it's fragile and doesn't work offline at all.
- **Invoice tools** — I use Wave for invoicing. Zero native connection. I manually copy project status updates between Notion and Wave, which is embarrassing honestly.

**Where Notion falls short compared to alternatives:**

Obsidian with community plugins handles local file connections beautifully — if I want something to talk to my local filesystem or a markdown-based tool, it just works, no API keys, no third-party middleware. Airtable, which I briefly used for client tracking, has far more robust native integrations and field type handling. It felt less pretty but way more dependable for actual data work.

Notion's integrations feel like they were designed by people who assume you have a stable broadband connection, an IT person, and patience for setup documentation. I have none of those things reliably.

---

## Q3: The One Connection I Actually Need

**Gmail, properly, natively.**

Not through Zapier. Not through a webhook I have to configure. I want to open a client's page in my Notion CRM and see the last three emails I exchanged with them. I want to log a reply and have it actually send from my Gmail. I want a little sidebar that says "this person emailed you 4 days ago and you haven't responded."

This exists in tools like HubSpot and even Notion-adjacent tools like Coda with some setup. But for someone like me — a freelancer whose entire business relationship history lives in email — the gap between Notion and my inbox is genuinely the biggest productivity hole I have.

I've looked at tools like Copper CRM specifically because of Gmail integration. The only reason I haven't switched my whole CRM workflow is that I don't want to fragment my knowledge base. But honestly? That calculus gets harder every month.

---

*The connectivity stuff isn't glamorous but it's where Notion quietly costs me the most time.*

---

**Q1: Last time Notion failed me offline**

About three months ago I was on a flight to our Denver office for an all-hands. I'd planned to use the flight time to finalize our IT onboarding documentation and review a compliance checklist I'd been building in Notion. Neither page loaded. I got the spinning indicator and then the "you're offline" screen. No cached content, nothing. I ended up working in a Google Doc I happened to have open from a previous session and then manually reconciling the changes afterward. That reconciliation took 45 minutes that shouldn't have been necessary. The frustrating part is that this wasn't exotic behavior - I'd *been in those pages an hour before boarding*. There's no reliable signal about what's actually cached versus what isn't.

**Q2: How critical is offline access day-to-day**

Honestly, more critical than Notion seems to assume. I'm regularly in situations - travel, client sites with locked-down networks, our own server room which has spotty coverage - where I need to pull up runbooks, network diagrams, incident response procedures. These are exactly the documents where "sorry, you're offline" is the worst possible answer. For a tool positioning itself as enterprise-grade, the offline story is embarrassingly thin compared to Confluence, which at least gives you predictable local caching behavior.

**Q3: Lost work or sync issues**

Yes. This one still bothers me. We had a situation where two members of my team were editing the same incident postmortem document simultaneously - one through the web app, one through the desktop client that apparently hadn't fully synced. When the conflict resolved, we lost roughly 20 minutes of structured analysis. Notion's conflict resolution is essentially silent - it doesn't tell you there *was* a conflict, it just picks a version. For a postmortem document with specific timeline entries and action items assigned to people, that's not acceptable. We now have an informal rule that no one edits critical ops docs simultaneously, which defeats half the purpose of a collaborative tool.

**Q1: Describe a workflow where you needed Notion to connect to an external tool. How did that go?**

The clearest pain point was trying to build a reliable incident management workflow that bridged Notion and Jira. The idea was straightforward: when a Jira ticket reaches a certain status, automatically update a corresponding Notion page with resolution notes, owner, and timestamps. That way our ops runbooks stay current without manual copy-paste.

In practice it was a mess. The Notion API rate limits hit us almost immediately at our scale. We're pushing hundreds of updates daily and we kept running into 429 errors with no graceful backoff documentation that actually matched real-world behavior. We ended up building a queuing layer just to babysit the API — which is infrastructure we never had to build for Confluence's Jira integration, which is native and just *works*.

We also discovered that Notion's API doesn't expose certain block types consistently. We had automation break silently because a page template someone updated on the frontend suddenly had a block type the API didn't handle the same way. No alerting, no schema versioning. It just failed quietly.

---

**Q2: What integrations does your team rely on, and where does Notion fall short compared to alternatives?**

Our critical integrations are Jira, Salesforce, Okta for SSO, and a handful of internal APIs for asset management and compliance logging.

**Okta/SSO** — this actually works reasonably well for basic provisioning, but the SCIM implementation is limited. Deprovisioning lags, and we've had terminated employees retain access longer than our security policy allows because SCIM sync isn't real-time. With SharePoint and Entra ID, deprovisioning is near-instant. That's not a minor gap — that's an audit finding waiting to happen.

**Salesforce** — there's no native integration. We're duct-taping Zapier in the middle, which means every Salesforce account update that's supposed to sync context to our client-facing Notion workspace goes through a third-party service that adds latency, introduces another failure point, and creates a data residency question our legal team is not thrilled about.

**Jira** — the native Notion-Jira integration is cosmetic at best. You can embed a Jira issue link. That's not integration, that's a hyperlink. Confluence's deep Jira integration — inline issue creation, status rollups, live roadmap data — is genuinely miles ahead.

**Internal APIs** — Notion's API is REST-only, no webhooks that are truly production-reliable. We've had outbound webhooks miss events during Notion incidents with no replay mechanism. For a compliance-sensitive environment, that's unacceptable.

---

**Q3: If you could make Notion talk to any external service seamlessly, what would it be and why?**

Jira, without hesitation — but *real* Jira integration, not the current surface-level one. I want bidirectional sync where an engineering spec in Notion and its associated Jira epic are genuinely in sync. Status changes, assignees, sprint data — reflected in both directions, reliably, with conflict resolution. 

The reason this matters so much at our scale: we've tried to use Notion as the *source of truth* for project context and Jira as the execution layer. Right now those two systems are islands and engineers are manually bridging them, which means one of them is always stale. That erodes trust in both tools. A real integration would let us actually deliver on the "Notion as your company wiki" promise because the operational data would be live, not a snapshot someone remembered to update.

Salesforce is a close second. Our customer success team lives in Notion for account planning but their source data is in Salesforce. That gap costs real hours every week.

---

**SEVERITY: 8/10**
The integration gaps aren't theoretical — they've caused compliance gaps, engineer frustration, and redundant infrastructure build-out.

**FREQUENCY: 9/10**
Someone on my team is troubleshooting an integration failure or working around an API limitation basically every day.

**SWITCH_LIKELIHOOD: 6/10**
We're invested and migration costs are real. But if Atlassian improves Confluence's UX much more, that number moves to an 8 fast.

# Notion AI – IT Lead Perspective

---

**Q1: How do you currently use Notion AI, and where does it disappoint you?**

Honestly, Notion AI sits in a weird middle ground for us. My team uses it for things like summarizing long runbooks, drafting incident response templates, and cleaning up documentation that engineers wrote at 2am during an outage. For those narrow, single-document tasks it's *fine* — functional, saves maybe 20 minutes here and there.

Where it falls apart is anything requiring context. I asked it to help me draft a security policy update, and it had zero awareness of the related policies sitting three pages away in the same database. I had to manually paste context in like it was a generic ChatGPT wrapper. For a tool that *lives inside* our knowledge base, that's a fundamental miss. It should know our stack. It doesn't. It's also given me confidently wrong summaries of database-linked content — the kind of thing that would be embarrassing if a non-technical manager acted on it without verifying.

---

**Q2: Describe a scenario where you wished Notion could reason across your entire workspace.**

We had a compliance audit — SOC 2 Type II prep. We have policies, access control docs, vendor assessments, incident logs, and onboarding checklists spread across probably 40 different Notion pages and databases. I needed to identify gaps: places where our documented controls didn't match our actual procedures, or where a policy referenced a tool we'd deprecated.

I wanted to ask something like: *"Show me every control in our security policy framework that references Okta, and cross-reference it against our current vendor inventory and incident history."* That should be a natural AI query inside a knowledge tool at enterprise scale. Instead, I was exporting CSVs, pulling things into a spreadsheet, and doing it manually over two days. Two days. Notion AI was completely useless for that workflow because it can't hold the whole workspace in view simultaneously.

That's not a nice-to-have feature — that's the core value proposition of having one unified knowledge system.

---

**Q3: How does Notion AI compare to other AI tools you use in your workflow?**

We use GitHub Copilot for the engineering team, Microsoft Copilot through our M365 licensing, and a few engineers are running Claude or GPT-4 with custom internal tooling through our API layer.

Notion AI feels like the least mature of the group by a meaningful margin. Microsoft Copilot — and I'll be honest, I pushed back hard on rolling it out — actually does cross-document reasoning across Teams, SharePoint, and Outlook in ways that are practically useful. It's not perfect but it understands *relationships* between documents. Notion AI doesn't get close to that.

GitHub Copilot has a clear, scoped use case and executes on it reliably. Notion AI's use case *should* be equally clear — reason over your company knowledge — and it doesn't execute. The comparison that stings most: my engineers have built internal tools using the Notion API plus Claude that do better cross-workspace reasoning than Notion's native AI product. That's an embarrassing gap for Notion to have. We're essentially building around their AI because we can't trust it at the level compliance work demands.

---

SEVERITY: 6/10
FREQUENCY: 7/10
SWITCH_LIKELIHOOD: 5/10

> *Note on ratings: The severity isn't fully blocking because AI is still additive — we'd survive without it. But the frequency is high because we bump into its context limitations almost every day at our scale. Switch likelihood is moderate — Notion's structure and flexibility still has advantages, but Microsoft Copilot's cross-document capabilities make the Confluence/SharePoint ecosystem harder to dismiss every quarter.*
